target: AG1's claim that making Election Day a national holiday would remove scheduling barriers and give most voters uninterrupted time to vote.
objection: A federal holiday does not force private employers to close or give paid time off, so many low-wage workers in retail, restaurants, caregiving, and other service jobs would still be scheduled to work and face a wages-versus-voting tradeoff. The holiday could therefore shift the burden rather than eliminate the barrier, especially for the workers least able to absorb lost pay.

target: AG2's claim that a federal holiday would not reliably create uninterrupted voting time because employers are not required to provide paid leave or shut down.
objection: The relevant issue is not whether every employer is legally compelled to provide paid leave, but whether the holiday changes normal attendance expectations. AG1 argues that national holidays typically produce an economy-wide scheduling reset—schools close and many employers reduce operations—so voters get meaningful time to vote without having to secure special leave.

target: AG1's assumption that declaring a national holiday reliably reduces attendance requirements for most voters.
objection: A federal holiday is only a public designation and does not compel private employers to shut down or to give paid time off. Since retail, restaurant, caregiving, and other essential service jobs often continue operating, the holiday may fail exactly where scheduling flexibility is lowest, leaving many voters with the same day-of conflict and wages-versus-attendance tradeoff.

target: AG2's assumption that a holiday only matters if employers are legally forced to shut down or pay workers.
objection: The objection rests on too narrow a view of the scheduling barrier. AG1 argues that the barrier is the expectation of ordinary day-of attendance, and a holiday changes that expectation by making schools close, many employers alter schedules, and workplaces more willing to accommodate brief voting breaks, even without a federal paid-leave mandate.

target: AG2's view that employer shutdown or paid leave is the main factor determining whether people can vote.
objection: Many scheduling barriers come from coordinating work with school and caregiving responsibilities, not just employer rules. A national holiday would align with the no-school / no-regular-arrangements reality for families and caregivers, creating a practical window to vote even when employers are not legally required to grant paid time off.

target: AG2's claim that a holiday will not reliably reduce day-of scheduling conflicts because private employers still control schedules.
objection: AG1 points to international practice as evidence against that assumption: 27 of 36 OECD countries hold elections on weekends or holidays, showing that shifting elections off a normal work/school day is commonly treated as a workable way to improve access even in systems with private employers and ordinary scheduling demands.

target: AG2's claim that low-wage workers will still face required full-day attendance and therefore no real scheduling reset.
objection: AG1 argues that a federal holiday usually does create a day-of scheduling reset: schools close and many employers reduce hours or staffing, so a substantial share of workers are not required to attend their usual shifts. That means voting is less likely to be a wage-loss decision and more likely to occur during genuinely freer time.

target: AG1's claim that Election Day as a national holiday is the best policy because it increases turnout and addresses scheduling problems.
objection: Research indicates that an election holiday by itself is not an effective way to raise voter turnout compared with other reforms. A calendar change alone does not directly solve the broader barriers that suppress turnout, such as registration access, early voting availability, or concrete workplace rules.

target: AG2's claim that the holiday is low-impact, inefficient, and likely to disadvantage low-income workers.
objection: A national Election Day holiday would directly address the day-of attendance problem that prevents people from voting, especially for low-wage workers who cannot easily take time off. AG1 argues the holiday is not merely symbolic, because it changes the operating day for many schools and workplaces and is supported by broad public opinion and international practice.

target: AG1's assumption that a federal holiday meaningfully resets schedules for most voters without harming low-income workers.
objection: Because federal law does not require private employers to shut down or provide paid leave, many low-income workers in retail, restaurants, caregiving, and similar jobs would still have to work on the holiday. That means the holiday can preserve the same scheduling barrier in the form of lost wages or missed voting time, concentrating the burden on workers least able to absorb it.

target: AG2's claim that a holiday is low-impact and does not directly address the day-of scheduling conflict.
objection: AG1 says the holiday would reduce or pause normal attendance expectations for schools and many workplaces, giving millions of people real access to vote without special arrangements. In this view, the holiday is a substantive scheduling change, not a symbolic one, and it helps those with the least flexibility.

target: AG1's claim that a federal holiday meaningfully pauses the operating day for people least able to take time off.
objection: A federal holiday does not legally require private employers to stop operating or provide paid leave, so for many low-income workers the holiday changes the calendar more than their actual ability to vote. The barrier remains a wages-versus-attendance choice, especially in service-sector jobs that continue on holidays.

target: AG2's argument that a federal holiday cannot meaningfully reduce the day-of conflict because private employers are not forced to close.
objection: AG1 responds that when Election Day is placed on a federal holiday, schools close and many employers reduce or alter operations, which lowers attendance expectations and makes voting more feasible for millions. The holiday also aligns with international practice and the needs of workers who have limited ability to take time off.

target: AG1's claim that the holiday would not disadvantage low-income workers.
objection: Even with a holiday, low-income workers may still have to choose between losing pay and voting, because many private employers—especially in retail, restaurants, caregiving, and other service jobs—can continue operating and scheduling staff. So the holiday can end up disproportionately burdening the very voters it is supposed to help.
